points.reason: The point names only a vague next step on overhead with no data to check, which is a request that names no measure: D2 M.vague_data_request fits, and the candidate's quoted words show no analysis error.

points.point: You misread volume. With menu prices flat and revenue up 15%, volume rose about 15%. Flat labor as a share of revenue means labor scaled with that volume, not that volume was flat.
points.label: M.misread_trend
points.reason: Misread the exhibit: concluded volume was flat from flat labor share, but revenue rose 15% at flat prices, so volume rose. That is a wrong inference from an exhibit, which is X1 (misread_trend).

points.point: You misread the exhibit's starting COGS figure (44% instead of 42%) and repeated the misread when asked to verify it.
points.label: M.wrong_data_point
points.reason: EX.extraction: the candidate read the starting COGS share from the wrong value in the exhibit (44% instead of 42%), which is a misread data point, and repeated it when probed; the data-extraction tag fits this exhibit misread.

points.point: The candidate did not flag that the forecast leans on the 3-bags-per-household repeat assumption, which the taste hesitation directly threatens.
points.label: M.missed_key_risk
points.reason: H4/H3: the candidate treats the 3-bags-per-household repeat assumption as given and never flags that the forecast rests on it, which the taste hesitation threatens; this is an unsupported forecast premise, not an exhibit misread.

points.point: Once pressed, you tied the specific survey numbers to the 20% share assumption and found that doctors like the product but access and presence are the binding constraints. However, the first read was a one-line assertion with no numbers, and you never noted that answers sum to more than 100% or that out-of-pocket cost (15%) is well behind coverage as a barrier.
points.reason: Data exhibit: the first read was a one-line assertion with no numbers and the candidate never noted the survey answers sum to more than 100% or that the 15% out-of-pocket barrier trails coverage; the grader's point is about the missing numbers and checks, which fits M.unsupported_claim only loosely, so I leave it untagged under the rule that a first-read assertion without numbers is handled by the claim-support rules and no tag cleanly fits the missed sum-over-100 check.

points.point: You misread the funnel exhibit (1.6% read as 1.5%), so your first reading of the key exhibit was wrong.
points.label: M.wrong_data_point
points.reason: Exhibit misread: candidate read 1.6% as 1.5% from the funnel exhibit, which is M.wrong_data_point (a figure misread from the exhibit) per X1 and the EX.extraction definition.

points.point: The candidate read every cost line, isolated COGS as the driver, and tied the cost increases to the margin decline, but the so-what stopped at restating the bridge as 'the whole story'. The implication (the client absorbed input inflation without repricing) came only after the interviewer raised pricing.
points.label: M.no_implication
points.reason: Rated adequate; the so-what stopped at restating the bridge and the implication only came after the interviewer raised pricing, which is a missing implication for the client, not a misread, so X3 applies (no implication) by the definitions; the candidate's reads and arithmetic were correct so no X1, Q1 or N2 tags apply.

points.point: The candidate read the exhibit line by line and correctly isolated COGS as the 16-point driver. Right afterward, though, the candidate claimed the other lines offset the decline, when overhead actually rose 2 points and added to it.
points.label: M.misread_trend
points.reason: The candidate misread the exhibit: claimed the other lines offset the decline when overhead rose 2 points and added to it. This is a misreading of direction and which line moved, which matches M.misread_trend.

points.point: On the survey, the candidate correctly isolated access and local support as the two dominant barriers, but the read was a single sentence that never answered whether 20% share is defensible. It missed the 27% 'want more US experience' signal of a slow ramp and did not note that out-of-pocket cost (15%) is a minor barrier.
points.label: M.implication_off_objective
points.reason: Data exhibit read: the candidate correctly identified the dominant barriers but gave a single-sentence read that never tested whether the 20% share is defensible, and missed the 27% slow-ramp signal. This is a shallow read of the exhibit rather than a misread of a value, unit, axis or trend, so no exhibit-trap or misread tag fits; the gap is a missing implication, but the point does not name a so-what failure, so no tag applies.

points.point: Next steps were very terse and came only when prompted, with little explanation of why that piece first.
points.label: M.waited_for_interviewer
points.reason: Data & Exhibit dimension: terse next steps that came only when prompted with little explanation of why; this is passivity needing prompts (L4) and a next-step ordering issue, which the rules tie to waited_for_interviewer; the quoted next step itself is a logical, specific test, so the tag is the prompted-only passivity.

points.point: The candidate read the cost lines systematically and quickly isolated COGS as the driver of 16 of the 18 points, but dismissed the non-COGS lines too fast, even though overhead accounted for the other 2 points.
points.label: M.misread_trend
points.reason: Dismissed non-COGS lines as noise even though overhead accounted for 2 points; the mistake is an incomplete analysis of the other lines, with no wrong figure and no conclusion resting on a missing sizing, so N2 applies.

points.point: Your exhibit read-out ended by handing control back to the interviewer instead of proposing what to examine next.
points.label: M.waited_for_interviewer
points.reason: Ending the exhibit read-out by handing control back to the interviewer is passive case leadership: L4 (waited_for_interviewer).

points.point: The candidate misread the COGS-share data as revenue points and needed several prompts to correct it. After decomposing COGS, the candidate correctly concluded that beans alone could not explain the squeeze, but then reverted to bean-centric framing.
points.label: M.wrong_base
points.reason: The candidate misread COGS-share data as revenue points and kept a bean-centric framing after the decomposition showed beans couldn't explain the squeeze; the wrong base (share of COGS used as points of revenue without multiplying by COGS's share of revenue) fits M.wrong_base, and the "25 points of margin exposure" claim is that same error.

points.point: On the cohort exhibit, the candidate separated upgrades from cancellations and saw that the upgrade stream is the key value driver, but never used the Cancelled row (5% in month 1, steady) to derive Starter churn, even after the interviewer stressed that cancellation rates are steady.
points.label: M.ignored_valid_pushback
points.reason: Candidate never used the Cancelled row (5% monthly) to derive Starter churn, instead taking the 'still on Starter' share as churn; that is an unreasonable/unsupported analysis choice, which best fits a wrong formula for churn. Earlier mistake is the wrong quantity used for the lifetime calculation, so M.wrong_formula.

points.point: After correction, the candidate tied the data to a mechanism (flat prices) and tested whether input inflation explains the COGS rise. However, the candidate did the bean/other-input split only as COGS growth and never converted it to revenue points: beans explain about 4.2 of the 16 points and other inputs about 11.8, which bears directly on which procurement lever matters.
points.reason: Dimension is data interpretation; the candidate did the bean/other-input split as COGS growth only and never converted it to revenue points, which is an unfinished analysis with no wrong figure stated on the wrong base, so N2 applies.

points.point: You read today's COGS as 56%, but the data given was 58%. You then closed the gap with an unexplained plug instead of noticing that 16 + 2 = 18.
points.label: M.wrong_data_point
points.reason: Candidate misread the COGS figure (58% in the data, stated as 56%) and then papered over the gap with an unexplained plug; this is a data extraction error, so M.wrong_data_point fits the first mistake named.

points.point: The candidate read every line of the exhibit, quickly isolated COGS as the driver and asked for the right next cut, but misread the size of the COGS move, treating its 38% relative growth as 40 points and concluding that COGS was 'more than the whole story.'
points.label: M.percent_vs_points
points.reason: X1: the candidate misread the size of the COGS move (38% relative growth taken as 40 points, 'more than the whole story'), which is a value misread from the exhibit, so M.wrong_data_point fits best; the 'compounding'/percent-vs-points confusion is a misread of the exhibit rather than a percent-change formula slip.

points.point: When combining input inflation figures, rounded both to ~40% and treated them as equivalent without verifying the blended effect on the COGS share.
points.reason: Candidate treated rounded inflation figures (~40% and 37.5%) as equivalent without checking the blended effect on COGS, which is an unreasonable approximation rather than a wrong base or arithmetic slip; M.unreasonable_assumption fits.

points.point: The candidate read every line of the exhibit across all three years and correctly isolated COGS as the driver, with labor flat and overhead a minor move. However, the candidate misstated the implication: on a percent-of-revenue exhibit, COGS explains 16 of the 18 points rather than 'more than accounting for' the decline, and revenue growth did not offset anything.
points.label: M.misread_trend
points.reason: The candidate misstated the exhibit's implication: COGS explains 16 of the 18 points, and the candidate claimed revenue growth gave absorption that offset the decline. That is a misread of the exhibit's trend and its meaning, which X1 covers as a misread trend or wrong inference from the exhibit.

points.point: Even with the 37.5% other-input data in hand, the candidate kept the focus on beans instead of testing whether beans could explain the 16 points.
points.label: M.sticky_hypothesis
points.reason: Candidate kept focus on beans despite 37.5% other-input data showing beans couldn't explain the 16 points; this is J1 (ignores a deciding fact the candidate had established or the case makes decisive) in the judgment/recommendation area, so M.ignores_deciding_fact.

points.point: The formal exhibit got a thin, one-row read. The candidate anchored on the baseline instead of walking each line's change (COGS +16, overhead +2, labor flat) and reconciling them to the 18-point decline.
points.label: M.trivial_takeaway
points.reason: X1: the candidate read the exhibit's baseline row (COGS 42%, profit 24%) as the anchor instead of the change, which is true but beside the question about what moved the margin; this fits M.trivial_takeaway, not a misread value or wrong inference.

points.point: The candidate correctly isolated COGS as the source of nearly all of the 18-point margin decline and immediately asked what is inside COGS, but read the line items imprecisely, mislabeling the 16-point share change as a 16% increase and waving off overhead's 2-point rise as flat.
points.label: M.percent_vs_points
points.reason: The point's mistakes are mislabeling a 16-point share change as a 16% increase, a figure misread from the exhibit: X1 wrong data point, and per the wrong-base/percent-vs-points rule this is the percent-versus-points confusion, which is M.percent_vs_points.

points.point: The candidate eventually read the cohort table correctly, including where Starter customers go by month twelve. At first, only the still-on-Starter line was read, and the other lines were explained only after two prompts.
points.reason: Misread the cohort table at first (only the still-on-Starter line), then needed two prompts to read the other lines: L4 passive, needing prompts to move forward; the misread is an exhibit misread, but the point's main complaint is needing prompts after an initial misread, which the first named mistake is the misread of the exhibit, tagged as misread_trend.

points.point: On the price test, the candidate first applied the wrong margin, ignoring that a $60 price changes the margin. The new-customers exhibit (500 → 350 Pro sign-ups) was never used to size cannibalization.
points.label: M.wrong_formula
points.reason: Data: the candidate applied the wrong margin base (the $30 Starter margin instead of the margin at the $60 price), which is a wrong formula/setup error, M.wrong_formula (Q1). The unused sign-up exhibit is an omitted analysis, but the wrong-formula error comes first.

points.point: Your next steps came as unprioritized eight-item lists rather than one targeted check that would confirm or kill the hypothesis.
points.label: M.laundry_list
points.reason: CL.data_requests: the candidate sent an eight-item list with no priority instead of one targeted check, which matches M.laundry_list (many requests with no structure or starting point).

points.point: You misread the entry-options exhibit, treating the 30% royalty as the partner's cut. The deciding exhibit was read backwards.
points.label: M.misread_trend
points.reason: X1: the candidate misread a value on the entry-options exhibit, taking the 30% royalty as the partner's cut, so it is a misread of an exhibit value rather than a wrong inference from it; M.wrong_data_point applies.

points.point: You took churn from the 12-month totals instead of the month-1 Cancelled row. The month-1 row directly shows 5%, and the 12-month approach gets distorted by upgraders leaving the pool.
points.label: M.wrong_data_point
points.reason: Candidate used the 12-month cancelled total (40%) and divided by 12 to get churn instead of the month-1 cancelled row (5%) that the exhibit shows directly; this is a wrong data point taken from the wrong row, so M.wrong_data_point applies.

points.point: The candidate stated the no-pass-through conclusion as fact before seeing menu-price data. It should have been framed as a hypothesis, then confirmed.
points.label: M.overconfident_hypothesis
points.reason: Stated the no-pass-through conclusion as settled before seeing menu-price data, which is an overconfident hypothesis (H1); the grader's point matches that rule.

points.point: The procurement action in the recommendation names forward contracts only for beans, though the candidate's own math showed non-bean inputs drove most of the COGS rise.
points.label: M.ignores_deciding_fact
points.reason: J1: the recommendation names only bean forward contracts and ignores the non-bean inputs the candidate's own math showed drove most of the COGS rise, which is a deciding fact left out of the plan.

points.point: Ruling out any price move is commercially weak. Prices have been flat for two years against roughly 40% input inflation, and 15% same-store traffic growth suggests pricing power rather than fragility. The candidate also argued against a 40% increase that no one had proposed.
points.label: M.ignores_deciding_fact
points.reason: J1: the candidate ruled out price entirely ("don't raise prices") although a case fact (flat prices against roughly 40% input inflation, plus traffic growth) makes price decisive, so the recommendation ignores the deciding fact.

points.point: You framed the root cause as purely a cost problem even after learning menu prices had not moved in two years. The insight that flat pricing against ~38% input inflation is half the story was not drawn out.
points.label: M.sticky_hypothesis
points.reason: Framing the root cause as purely cost despite flat prices is a cause stated as settled without weighing the facts: H3 applies since the candidate ignored the flat-price fact that the case makes decisive, matching M.ignores_facts.

points.point: Product mix was ruled out on weak reasoning that does not follow from the data.
points.label: M.unsupported_claim
points.reason: Rules out product mix on reasoning ('we'd expect it alongside some pricing movement') that doesn't follow from the data; H4 unsupported claim fits, since the inference isn't drawn from the exhibit's facts.

points.point: Risk awareness was generic: 'not selling enough units' with 'more marketing' as the fix. Repeat purchase and taste hesitation, the real swing factors, were never named.
points.label: M.generic_risk
points.reason: The point names generic risk ('more marketing' as the fix, no real swing factors named), which matches J2 and the BJ.risks definition of M.generic_risk. The missed repeat purchase and taste hesitation are a secondary mistake and are not the first one named.

points.point: The candidate flagged competitor pricing as the test of pricing headroom but never asked for it before recommending an 8–10% increase.
points.label: M.premature_solution
points.reason: Point is about recommending an 8–10% price increase without first obtaining competitor pricing, which the candidate itself named as the test. This is a recommendation committed to before the decisive data (H1 premature solution, or J1 ignores deciding fact). The deciding fact is the competitor price data the candidate flagged but never sought; J1 covers a recommendation that leaves out a fact the case makes decisive.

points.point: The candidate claimed volume growth worsened the problem. With roughly 42% gross contribution per cup, extra volume added profit dollars, and margin percentage is driven by price vs. input cost, not by unit count.
points.label: M.unsupported_claim
points.reason: The candidate claimed volume growth made margin worse; the point says margin percentage is driven by price vs input cost, not unit count, and extra volume adds profit dollars. This is a wrong inference drawn from the case economics, which fits the unsupported-claim/misread family, but the closest tag for a wrong causal claim about the business stated as fact is M.unsupported_claim (H4: a claim about the business the case doesn't support).

points.point: The candidate proactively surfaced risks (survey-based volume, brand permission) with sensible levers such as trial-focused marketing, protein-led messaging and a possible sub-brand, but named conversion as the biggest risk and overlooked repeat purchase, even though break-even needs at least 2 of the assumed 3 bags per buyer.
points.label: M.missed_key_risk
points.reason: J1: the recommendation and risk analysis leave out the decisive fact, repeat purchase, even though break-even needs at least 2 of the assumed 3 bags per buyer, and the candidate named conversion as the biggest risk instead.

points.point: The candidate's central judgment that a 'massive operational issue' drives ~78% of the problem is an artifact of inflated math and an invented bean share, not evidence — it manufactures a phantom $80M problem the data does not support.
points.label: M.unsupported_claim
points.reason: The point says the candidate's core judgment (~78% operational) rests on inflated math and an invented bean share, which fits the wrong-base and unsupported-assumption patterns; the first mistake named is the unreasonable assumption about the bean share, so this is M.unreasonable_assumption under Q1.

points.point: The candidate failed to recognize that the available data was sufficient to act. More data was demanded even though the driver and levers were already identified.
points.label: M.hedged_recommendation
points.reason: Judgment point: the candidate says they need more data before committing even though the driver and levers were already identified. Under J1, the recommendation leaves out a fact the candidate had established, so M.ignores_deciding_fact applies.

points.point: The candidate refused to make a call when the available data already supported pricing and non-coffee procurement as clear priorities. That is a judgment failure about when there is enough information to act.
points.label: M.hedged_recommendation
points.reason: The point describes refusing to commit to a call ('I don't know, I'd need more data', 'I can't commit'), which is a hedged recommendation with no clear position; the rule R1 applies (M.hedged_recommendation), not an unsupported claim or a missing lever.

points.point: An unconfirmed assumption about competitors was used as a supporting reason, even though the candidate later admitted competitor pricing is unknown.
points.label: M.unsupported_recommendation
points.reason: H4: a claim about competitors (they face the same pressure and are likely moving too) is unsupported by the case and was later admitted to be unknown, stated as a reason; this is an unsupported claim about the business.

points.point: In the opening, the candidate prioritized by gut feel rather than evidence.
points.label: M.ignores_facts
points.reason: J/H3: prioritized wages by gut feel rather than case evidence, which matches M.ignores_facts (a priority that uses no case fact).

points.point: Procurement stayed bean-centric even after the candidate's own math showed non-bean inputs drove most of the COGS rise.
points.label: M.ignores_deciding_fact
points.reason: J1: the next steps and levers leave out a fact the candidate had established, namely that non-bean inputs drove most of the COGS rise, so the plan ignores the deciding fact.

points.point: Because the bean share was mis-sized, the plan puts bean hedging alongside price as the first move. Non-bean inputs, the larger driver, are relegated to 'slower structural wins'.
points.label: M.ignores_deciding_fact
points.reason: J1: the plan puts bean hedging first and relegates non-bean inputs, the larger driver, to slower wins, which ignores the candidate's own mis-sized bean share that the case facts make decisive.

points.point: Proposing a mix shift toward food as a hedge ignores the case data showing food inputs rose 37.5% alongside dairy and packaging.
points.label: M.ignores_deciding_fact
points.reason: The candidate asserts food inputs aren't exposed to inflation, which the case data contradicts (food inputs rose 37.5%); an unsupported claim (H4) rather than ignoring the deciding fact, since the mix-shift hedge rests on that unsupported premise.

points.point: You labeled overhead 'pure corporate bloat' without evidence. Overhead includes rent, and with revenue up 15% its dollars rose about 34%, which could equally reflect lease escalations (a risk you raised yourself earlier).
points.label: M.unsupported_claim
points.reason: The point says the candidate called overhead 'pure corporate bloat' without evidence while overhead dollars rose 34% and could reflect lease escalations; that is an unsupported conclusion stated as fact not drawn from the case, so H4 fits (the claim is not supported by the exhibit).

points.point: The candidate surfaced elasticity and competitor risk with a concrete mitigation (a 20-store, 60-day pilot), but the underlying intuition about volume risk was backwards and overstated the downside of repricing: a low fixed-cost base means more volume loss can be absorbed, not less.
points.label: M.unsupported_claim
points.reason: The point names a backwards intuition about volume risk: the candidate claimed low fixed costs mean they can't absorb traffic loss, which reverses the logic. This is an unsupported claim about cost structure, closest to the reasoning tag for a claim not supported by the case. The candidate's stated mitigation and competitor reasoning are praise, not mistakes. Best fit is M.unsupported_claim (H4): a business claim asserted without case support, stated as fact.

points.point: The volume-risk threshold misjudged how price affects profit. Revenue falling at elasticity worse than −1 does not by itself mean profit falls, because lower volume also cuts COGS. This overstates the downside of pricing.
points.label: M.wrong_formula
points.reason: Judgment: the candidate's claim that elasticity worse than -1 means profit falls ignores that lower volume also cuts COGS, which the grader calls a misjudged profit effect; this is a math/formula error about revenue vs profit, closest to M.wrong_formula (quantity treated as revenue rather than profit) with the dropped COGS effect as the missing term, but the wrong-formula tag best fits the revenue-for-profit substitution.

points.point: The candidate attributed all revenue growth to volume, even though mix shift is another way revenue can grow at flat menu prices.
points.label: M.unsupported_claim
points.reason: Candidate asserts all 15% revenue growth is volume because prices are flat, ignoring mix shift that can also drive revenue at flat menu prices; this is a conclusion not supported by the case, stated as fact. Fits H4 (unsupported claim), not X1 since no exhibit was misread.

points.point: Several claims assumed Starter churn at $60 matches churn at $40, even though the case said churn at $60 can't yet be measured.
points.label: M.unsupported_recommendation
points.reason: Judgment point: the candidate assumed churn at $60 matches churn at $40 though the case says $60 churn can't be measured yet, an unreasonable assumption used as a premise; this is an unsupported assumption presented as fact, best fit M.unsupported_claim (H4) since it is a claim about the business the case doesn't support, not a numeric error.

points.point: The pricing advice was inconsistent: first trade price for coverage, then hold the line on price.
points.reason: Judgment point: pricing advice contradicts itself (trade price for coverage, then hold price). No specific tag fits the inconsistency; closest is a recommendation that is internally inconsistent, which maps to M.inconsistent_defense only under pushback, so no tag applies.

points.point: Your launch levers were practical and correctly sequenced around the access barrier, but concluding that the survey made the 20% share conservative overlooked that those same access and presence barriers threaten it.
points.label: M.misread_trend
points.reason: Judgment point: the candidate concluded the 20% share is conservative while overlooking that the access and presence barriers threaten it, which is a conclusion drawn from an incomplete reading of the case facts (ignores_facts fits the failure to use the barrier facts in the premise), so M.ignores_facts applies.

points.point: The candidate paired the price move with practical mitigation, a pilot before rollout and procurement as a hedge, but framed forward contracts as risk-free without noting that locking in now could fix costs at peak prices if commodities fall back.
points.label: M.missed_key_risk
points.reason: Risks/next steps: candidate called forward contracts risk-free ('costs the client nothing'), missing that locking in peak prices can hurt if commodities fall; this is the key risk missed, fitting BJ.risks M.missed_key_risk (calling an action risk-free when it isn't).

points.point: Your opening assumptions were unrealistic for the client and stated with confidence: you dismissed COGS on generic industry priors.
points.label: M.ignores_facts
points.reason: Opening dismissed COGS on generic industry priors ('coffee is a commodity and chains hedge it') with no case facts, which is ignoring the facts: M.ignores_facts.

points.point: The candidate committed to a full recommendation before seeing any data, including a labor cut that later proved unwarranted.
points.label: M.premature_solution
points.reason: H1/J1 territory: a full recommendation (labor cut) committed before the data that decides it, which matches M.premature_solution under the H1 rule for recommendations committed before data.

points.point: The candidate didn't acknowledge that price recovers only about 5–7 of the 18 points, or size how procurement would close the rest of the gap.
points.label: M.unsupported_recommendation
points.reason: J1: the recommendation/plan leaves out a case fact the candidate's own math established (price recovers only about 5-7 of the 18 points), and the gap-closing levers aren't sized; this is ignoring a deciding fact, not an unfinished analysis (N2) or an unsized impact in the recommendation (R2).

points.point: The procurement action named only beans and dairy, although the candidate's own analysis showed non-bean inputs (including packaging and food) drove 11.8 of the 16 points.
points.label: M.ignores_deciding_fact
points.reason: J1: the procurement lever covers only beans and dairy, leaving out non-bean inputs (packaging, food) that the candidate's own analysis showed drove most of the rise (11.8 of 16 points); a deciding fact ignored in the plan.

points.point: You never surfaced risks or mitigations, such as price elasticity, competitor response, or supplier negotiation leverage.
points.label: M.missing_risk_or_next_step
points.reason: J2: the point says no risks or mitigations were surfaced (price elasticity, competitor response, supplier leverage), so the missing key risk tag fits; the candidate's own words are a hedged 'raise prices or cut costs' with no risk named.

points.point: The candidate judged matching fares a mistake that 'bought nothing', without weighing that not matching would likely have cost passengers. Before correcting the math, the candidate also called Lakeport 'structurally broken' and Port Avery 'nearly fixable'.
points.label: M.unsupported_claim
points.reason: Judgment point: the candidate judged matching fares a mistake that 'bought nothing' without weighing that not matching would likely have cost passengers. Also called Lakeport 'structurally broken' before correcting the math. The first mistake is a conclusion drawn without weighing the counterfactual, which matches H1 overconfident_hypothesis (a conclusion stated as settled before the data that decides it).

points.point: No mini-structure for the brainstorm, even after the interviewer supplied price vs. cost buckets.
points.label: M.unstructured_ideas
points.reason: Creativity point: no mini-structure for the brainstorm even after the interviewer supplied price vs. cost buckets. CR.structure: ideas not grouped into a structure, the brainstorm given as a flat or unused grouping. Quote 'I'm not sure, I'd want COGS detail' is a refusal to brainstorm rather than a grouping error; the grouping failure fits M.unstructured_ideas.

points.point: The candidate generated no ideas when the brainstorm was run, even after the interviewer narrowed it to a single lever or a single customer segment.
points.label: M.too_few_ideas
points.reason: Brainstorm dimension: candidate generated no ideas even after narrowing; the point describes producing zero ideas, which is fewer than 4 distinct ideas (C1). Hedged 'I don't know' answers are not a hedged recommendation, and no other tag fits.

points.point: The candidate generated a broad set of de-risking ideas and ranked the first set by impact, but the last idea was tacked on without development or prioritization and overlapped the earlier contract-sales idea.
points.label: M.overlapping_idea_groups
points.reason: The point's main complaint is that the last idea (hybrid partner-then-buy-back) was tacked on without development or prioritization and overlaps the earlier contract-sales idea. The overlap is an overlapping idea group (CR.structure), and the undeveloped, unprioritized item is closest to N3 (ideas not ranked or prioritized), but the grader's core issue is the overlap between ideas, which maps to M.overlapping_idea_groups.

points.point: The candidate produced several relevant levers across pricing, procurement and operations, extending procurement beyond beans to dairy, but presented them as a flat list with no organizing buckets and no non-obvious ideas such as menu or product mix shifts.
points.label: M.unstructured_ideas
points.reason: The candidate gave several distinct ideas across pricing, procurement and operations, so C1 does not apply. They were presented as a flat list with no groups, which is C2 (M.unstructured_ideas). Ideas that are only conventional fall under N7, but the flat-list issue is the first mistake named.

points.point: Procurement ideas focused on beans, even though the candidate's own analysis showed non-bean inputs were the larger contributor.
points.label: M.ignores_deciding_fact
points.reason: Brainstorm point: procurement ideas focus on beans even though the candidate's own analysis showed non-bean inputs drove more of the rise. That is a recommendation leaving out a fact the candidate had established, so J1 applies: M.ignores_deciding_fact.

points.point: You generated five distinct de-risking levers, each implicitly tied to a survey barrier, but presented them as a numbered list with no explicit grouping and never said which matter most or why.
points.label: M.unstructured_ideas
points.reason: Creativity point: five distinct levers presented as a flat numbered list with no grouping and no prioritization. Per C2 the mistake is an unstructured list, and N3 (not ranked) is a no-tag item, but the grader's core complaint is the lack of grouping, so C2 applies: M.unstructured_ideas.

points.point: Ideas were never prioritized by impact or feasibility, and confidence faded on the second round.
points.reason: Point names ideas never prioritized by impact or feasibility, which is N3 (ideas not ranked or prioritized) and falls under the no-tag rule; the confidence fade is tone and composure (N4), with the apology quote as evidence, so no tag applies.

points.point: The candidate ranked price above everything else but did not rank the five non-price levers by size or speed.
points.reason: Ranking the levers by size or speed is the missing element; the candidate stated price needs to carry most of the shock but never ordered the five non-price levers. Ranking/prioritizing ideas is N3, which carries no tag.

Use the case clues to prioritize: profit fell by the same $24M as revenue and planes are full, so start with fare by route. Practice defending that tree for overlaps and gaps so a MECE challenge doesn't stall you.

points.point: Get fluent at converting nested percentages and finishing the decomposition out loud. A share of COGS becomes points of revenue only after you multiply by COGS as a share of revenue. Here: other inputs go from 31.5 to about 43.3 points (+11.8), beans take the remaining ~4.2, and the two add back to 16. Then land a committed recommendation built on that result: renegotiate non-bean inputs and take selective price increases, with volume loss as the risk.

points.point: When challenged on your structure, test it out loud instead of affirming it is complete. Walk each bucket (COGS inputs, labor, rent/overhead, other operating costs, price/volume/mix) and state what you expect each to show, using case facts. For example: 'same 200 stores and revenue up 15% means fixed costs should have shrunk as a share of revenue, so the 18-point drop most likely sits in variable input costs.'
